t:
(a) In General.—All regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions described under subsection (b) shall remain in effect according to the terms of such regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions, and shall be enforceable by or against the Director until modified, terminated, set aside, or superseded in accordance with applicable law by the Director, any court of competent jurisdiction, or operation of law. 
    (b) Applicability.—A regulation, order, determination, or resolution is described under this subsection if it—
        (1) was issued, made, prescribed, or allowed to become effective by—
            (A) the Board; or 
            (B) a court of competent jurisdiction, and relates to functions transferred by this Act; and  
        (2) is in effect on the effective date of the abolishment under section 1311(a).

fable.w: This is a savings clause that keeps existing regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions of the abolished Board in force after its functions transfer to the Director. The tempting reading is that the references to regulations, to courts, and to enforceability "against the Director" signal rulemaking or a right to sue. That fails because the section neither requires or authorizes new rulemaking nor grants any outside party a new right to challenge a federal decision. It only preserves the legal status quo, and no party outside the federal government is consulted or involved in a decision.
fable.s: shall remain in effect according to the terms of such regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions, and shall be enforceable by or against the Director until modified, terminated, set aside, or superseded

qwen_block.w: This section describes the legal status and enforceability of existing regulations and orders following a transfer of functions. It does not establish any process for outside parties to consult with, advise, or participate in the decision-making process of the federal government. The mention of courts refers to judicial review/enforcement, which is a trap for 'granting the right to sue' only if the text explicitly grants a new right to sue; here it merely states existing orders are enforceable by courts, which is a standard legal provision, not a participation mechanism.
qwen_block.s: All regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions described under subsection (b) shall remain in effect according to the terms of such regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions, and shall be enforceable by or against the Director until modified, terminated, set aside, or superseded in accordance with applicable law by the Director, any court of competent jurisdiction, or operation of law.

opus.w: This savings clause only keeps existing regulations, orders, determinations and resolutions in effect after the Board is abolished and its functions move to the Director. Mentioning regulations and courts that may set them aside is tempting. But the section doesn't authorize new rulemaking, require public comment or consultation, or give any outside party a new right to sue. It just refers to whatever 'applicable law' already provides, so no outside party is brought into a federal decision.
opus.s: shall be enforceable by or against the Director until modified, terminated, set aside, or superseded in accordance with applicable law by the Director, any court of competent jurisdiction, or operation of law.
opus.b:
I'd label this section **No**. It's a savings clause that keeps existing regulations and orders in force; it doesn't set up any process that involves people outside the federal government.

**The tempting reading:** The section mentions "regulations" and says rules can be "set aside" by "any court of competent jurisdiction." That could look like it requires rulemaking or gives outsiders a right to sue. It does neither. It only keeps the Board's existing regulations, orders and court rulings in effect after the Board is abolished. Any later change must happen "in accordance with applicable law." That points to procedures set elsewhere and doesn't create a new rulemaking duty, comment period, hearing, or right to sue. The only actors named are the Director, the former Board and courts, all inside the government.

qwen_chat.w: This section is a standard continuity provision stating that existing regulations remain in effect until changed by the agency head, a court, or operation of law. It does not establish a new process for outside parties to consult with the government, nor does it grant a specific right to sue or participate in decision-making. The mention of a court is descriptive of existing legal mechanisms for enforcement or invalidation, not a grant of participatory rights.
qwen_chat.s: All regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions described under subsection (b) shall remain in effect according to the terms of such regulations, orders, determinations, and resolutions, and shall be enforceable by or against the Director until modified, terminated, set aside, or superseded in accordance with applicable law by the Director, any court of competent jurisdiction, or operation of law.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text mentions a "court of competent jurisdiction" and the ability to have regulations "set aside," this implies a right to sue or judicial review, which is a form of participation. However, the text merely states that existing regulations remain enforceable until changed by the Director, a court, or operation of law. It does not grant a new right to sue, nor does it describe a process for outside parties to participate in the creation or modification of these regulations. It is a boilerplate provision regarding the continuity of law during an agency transition.
